context: The diagram analyzes heap construction on a perfect binary tree of height h. Select nodes from the bottom up and sift each one down. Bottom-up describes the order in which nodes are selected. Each repair still proceeds toward the children.

The tree is on the left. On the right, the columns show “Node height (maximum heapify iterations)” and “Nodes per level.” Horizontal dashed lines align the levels. Leaves have height 0 and the root has height h. Height counts edges to the deepest leaf below a node. The iteration count here is the maximum number of downward swaps, excluding the code's final stopping check.
description: Let the root be at depth 0 and the leaves at depth h. Level d contains 2 to the power d nodes, each of which can sink at most h−d levels. Multiplying these gives the bound for that level. Charging every node the root height h overestimates the work because about half the nodes are leaves and never sink.

The diagram shows the first four levels and the last two, with a vertical ellipsis between them. The table adds the depth, general formula, and product. For small h, count only levels that exist, and count overlapping first and last rows only once.

frames.explanation: The node counts and maximum levels per node come from the two columns in the diagram. The table adds the depths and the calculated upper bound for each level. In practice, sifting can stop before reaching the bound if the heap property already holds.
frames.title: Work per level when building a heap

result: Summing over levels gives T(h) = 2^0×h + 2^1×(h−1) + … + 2^(h−1)×1 + 2^h×0. The shift-and-subtract calculation below gives T(h) = 2^(h+1) − h − 2. Since the tree has n = 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes, T(h) = n − h − 1. Including the linear overhead of checking the nodes, building the heap takes O(n) time.
summary: The lower levels contain many nodes, but each can sink only a few levels. Counting the work level by level gives a linear time bound.
